articles.snippet: Exit strategies: When to sell and not to sell  Silicon Valley Bank

post1.text:
Most business owners think they sell their company. The truth is, buyers buy a multiple. And most founders at the $50M to $500M level have no idea what's actually driving that number.

A recent U.S. Chamber of Commerce piece on exit strategy reinforces something we see constantly: leaders wait too long to think about this. By the time they're ready to sell, the window to improve their multiple has already closed.

Here's what actually moves the needle before you go to market:

Revenue quality matters more than revenue size. Recurring, predictable income streams command higher multiples than lumpy project-based revenue, even at the same top line.

Customer concentration is a quiet killer. If your top three clients represent more than 40% of revenue, expect buyers to price that risk aggressively.

Leadership depth is valued like an asset. A business that runs without the owner is worth significantly more than one that doesn't.

You don't need to be exiting tomorrow to start optimizing for a sale. In fact, the best outcomes come from founders who start three to five years out.

So here's the real question: if a buyer walked in tomorrow, what would they see that would scare them off?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur makes a point that every founder at scale needs to hear: growth planning and exit planning are not the same discipline, and treating them as if they are is one of the most expensive mistakes a business owner can make.

At Autobahn, we work with companies in the $50M to $500M range, and this gap shows up constantly. Leaders pour energy into top-line growth while leaving value on the table because the business was never structured with a transaction in mind.

The fix is not complicated, but it does require starting earlier than feels necessary. Buyers reward businesses that are already clean, scalable, and owner-independent before the conversation begins.

If you are building toward an eventual exit, read this one. Then ask your team whether your current growth strategy is also an exit strategy.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMilAFBVV95cUxNQ1IwcXAwLW0wOUR3UTROejNURE9ORVB1NmdRRi1Ccm4wbjdRa2Rrcy05R3h0OTJkT0xrV2paVENfblRqRHVsZFVKZHJ2cDFTalhCcWpVc2J6YlBkeDNBMm1fUWE3dmRzY2ZtRkduR3lvQnFRVDFJMnNtTloyd0xSUlhFNDg2WmxZNFl1TzhuNEU4WUpB

post3.text:
Silicon Valley Bank recently published a piece on exit strategy timing, specifically the tension between knowing when to sell and knowing when to hold. It is a real dilemma, and most founders navigate it without a clear framework.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles exactly this. Titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, and authored by Paul Belair and George Hohman, the chapter goes beyond the obvious advice and gets into the specific levers that determine what a buyer will actually pay for your business.

One thing Paul and George make clear: your multiple is not set at the negotiating table. It is set years earlier, in the decisions you make about structure, customers, and leadership. Most owners discover this too late.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because execution never had a real owner.

Companies scaling past $50M tend to invest heavily in planning retreats, slide decks, and quarterly reviews. Then the plan sits in a shared drive and life moves on. The African food sector is a vivid example of this: analysts point out that the continent's food future will not be determined by ideas or ambition, but by who actually shows up in markets, secures financing, and executes with discipline.

Three things scaling companies consistently get wrong:

1. Strategy and operations are treated as separate conversations instead of one continuous loop.
2. Accountability is assigned to teams instead of specific individuals with decision-making authority.
3. Milestones exist on paper but are never tied to resource allocation.

A plan without a named owner is just a wish list.

Who in your organization is truly accountable for making your strategy move, not just monitoring it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in African Business made a sharp observation: the future of Africa's food industry will be decided not by vision, but by who wins in markets, finance, and execution.

That framing applies directly to any company navigating aggressive growth.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this constantly with companies scaling from $50M upward. Leaders arrive with strong strategies and sharp market insight. What stalls them is the gap between a well-articulated plan and the operational infrastructure needed to run it at scale. Execution is not a soft skill. It is a system, and it requires deliberate design.

If your team can articulate the strategy but struggles to describe who owns what by when, that gap is costing you growth.

Read the full article and think about where your own execution breaks down: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiswFBVV95cUxNZTdwdjlOekkzYWg2MTB5THdxWWtMR3ZHWmhNcmRmSnV3NDViZE02T0VVdGhXc1N4R2VEZklCTU1pV3lrNmoxT1FOdFdGTUpZSktSa2V0NXVaNmpMdjItdUFyNXg3TVlTckh5N3lzdllrOHJnQmR3V2Z3OWM2Q3pYaU1rVWdCRVFoXzg4MVNqR2E5QjNoMG0tX1lBdVRYM3FXcFczZDd4V3FNT1MtakRyRlozTQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Strategy without execution is noise. That is the hard truth sitting at the center of Chapter 3 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business.

The chapter is titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," and it was written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall. It draws on real business experience across wildly different industries to show that the fundamentals of strategic execution are not industry-specific. They are universal.

One of the core insights Rafa and Jim surface: the companies that scale successfully are not necessarily the ones with the best plans. They are the ones that build cultures where follow-through is non-negotiable, not optional.

This is not theory. It is hard-won pattern recognition from people who have lived it.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies above $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. Habits are what your team does when no one is watching. Strategy is a deliberate set of choices about where to compete, who to target, and how to win. Confusing the two is expensive.

McKinsey recently confirmed what we see in the field: the growth threshold for B2B companies has shifted dramatically. Standing still isn't neutral anymore. Companies that lack a defined, repeatable sales motion are effectively funding their competitors' growth.

Here's what that means in practice for leaders at your stage:

1. Revenue that feels consistent is often just momentum from decisions made two years ago.
2. Hiring more salespeople without a clear strategy accelerates the wrong behaviors.
3. The gap between $50M and $200M is almost never a market problem. It's a sales architecture problem.

What would your revenue look like if your team executed a real strategy instead of just following routines?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Gartner makes a point that every chief sales officer needs to sit with: AI is saving sales reps time, but that time is not automatically turning into revenue. CSOs who assume efficiency gains will self-convert into pipeline are going to be disappointed.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly in scaling companies. Leaders invest in tools that reduce friction, then wait for growth that never arrives. The missing ingredient is always intentional direction from the top.

If your sales team has more capacity but flat results, the problem is not your tech stack. It is the absence of a strategy that tells your team exactly what to do with the time they just got back.

Read the full Gartner piece and then ask yourself honestly: do your reps know where to focus? https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that opens with a line that stops leaders cold: every day without a real sales strategy is a donation.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business, written by Deb and Brandon, is titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation. It was written for companies that are already generating revenue and still losing ground, not because they lack talent, but because their sales effort has never been built into a true strategy.

The chapter tackles something that recent research from McKinsey reinforces: B2B growth now requires more than activity. It requires architecture. Deb and Brandon lay out a framework for what that actually looks like inside a company at the $50M to $500M stage.

The insight that tends to land hardest with leaders? It involves what you are measuring versus what actually predicts growth.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they walk away from any interaction with your company.

Most $50M+ leaders obsess over marketing spend and channel mix. Very few ask the harder question: what does our brand actually make people feel?

Adweek recently examined how Campari manages a portfolio of iconic brands across generations and markets. The throughline was not advertising budget. It was intentional culture work that shapes how every brand shows up consistently over time.

Three things scaling companies consistently get wrong on this:

1. They treat brand as a design project, not a strategic one. Your positioning decisions belong in the boardroom, not just the creative suite.

2. They let the brand drift as they add headcount. Every new hire is either reinforcing your brand or diluting it.

3. They confuse awareness with preference. Getting noticed and getting chosen are two completely different problems.

If your company doubled in size tomorrow, would your brand still feel like yours?

#BrandStrategy #ScalingBusiness #MarketingLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention. The core argument: brand building and performance marketing are not opposing forces. The companies winning right now are the ones treating them as one integrated system.

This matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M range. At that stage, most leaders are still running brand and demand generation as separate budgets with separate teams and separate goals. That structure creates real blind spots.

When brand and channel strategy are disconnected, you end up spending on acquisition while quietly eroding the trust that makes acquisition stick.

The smartest scaling companies we work with have stopped asking 'brand or performance?' and started asking 'how does each reinforce the other?'

Worth a read if you are rethinking how your marketing dollars are organized: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
Campari has spent decades managing beloved brands without letting them go stale or lose their identity. The question they keep answering is one every scaling company needs to face: as you grow, how do you keep your brand from becoming generic?

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is called 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' and it is written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West.

The chapter title is intentional. Brand is sensory before it is rational. People experience your company before they can articulate what they think about it. Kayli and Yasmin give leaders a concrete way to audit what their brand is actually communicating versus what they believe it is communicating.

There is a gap in most companies between intended brand and lived brand. Chapter 5 shows you how to close it.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at $50M and above are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. Hootsuite recently published a list of 31 social media metrics worth tracking. Thirty-one. For one channel. That number tells you everything about where we are headed if we are not careful.

Here is what we see repeatedly with scaling companies:

First, when every metric matters, none of them do. Leaders stop acting because they cannot determine which number to trust.

Second, KPIs get added but never retired. The dashboard grows. Clarity shrinks.

Third, the metrics being tracked often reflect activity, not outcomes. Busy work gets measured. Progress does not.

The companies that scale well pick a small number of indicators that directly connect to revenue, customer retention, or operational health. Then they hold the line against adding more.

How many of the KPIs on your dashboard would you eliminate if you had to cut the list in half?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite breaks down 30 financial metrics and KPIs worth tracking in 2026. It is a solid reference, and for companies in early growth stages, that kind of comprehensive list has real value.

But for companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, the challenge is not knowing which metrics exist. It is ruthless prioritization.

At that revenue level, your reporting infrastructure is usually outpaced by your growth. Executives pull from multiple sources. Numbers conflict. Meetings stall because no one agrees on the baseline.

The fix is not more dashboards. It is organizational alignment around a shorter, non-negotiable set of financial indicators that every leader reads the same way.

If your team cannot recite your top five financial KPIs without looking them up, that is the real problem.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikwFBVV95cUxNcThuZllxNkVka0dpOV9QdHZQM2RiU0tfMGVIR05tdW9ZN1AtYngwQ1d4WDFSb3ZNSUxKNHFCSUR4aC1lR1g2ZWYzWFE0NWF1WmVpejAxOW9VRFdJa01yLUFKa1hvbjNGQnR6a2hZcVVtQzgwRXNCdXVGbjhfNWR2eWpTSlFyRk5zLVZ3MnJvMU14ZjA

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that starts with a question most executives are afraid to answer honestly: how many of your KPIs has anyone actually acted on in the last 90 days?

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled Death by KPIs. It was written by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it goes directly at one of the most common traps growing companies fall into. The bigger you get, the more metrics accumulate. The more metrics accumulate, the less anyone is accountable for any single one.

The chapter does not just diagnose the problem. It gives leadership teams a way to cut through the noise and identify which numbers actually drive the business forward at scale.

If your team is tracking everything and moving nothing, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong, and the productivity numbers prove it.

A recent Fortune survey found that 90% of executives say AI has not meaningfully boosted productivity at their companies. That is not an AI problem. That is a deployment problem.

Here is what leaders at scaling companies need to understand:

First, AI does not fix broken processes. It accelerates them, good or bad. If your operations have inefficiencies at $50M, AI will make those inefficiencies faster and more expensive.

Second, the companies seeing real gains are not using AI as a novelty. They are assigning it specific, repeated, high-volume tasks where the output is measurable.

Third, ROI from AI does not show up on a dashboard after week one. The leaders winning with AI right now set a 90-day baseline before they judge results.

The question is not whether AI belongs in your business. It is whether your business is structured to absorb it.

What does AI accountability actually look like inside your organization today?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune stopped us in our tracks: 90% of executives say AI has not improved productivity at their companies, and some are still cutting jobs in the hope that AI will eventually fill the gap.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth stage, this is a critical warning sign.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern often. Leaders adopt AI tools before they have defined what success looks like. No baseline. No accountability. No process owner. The tool becomes shelf software with a subscription fee.

If you are scaling right now, the real competitive advantage is not having AI. It is knowing exactly where AI fits in your business and measuring it like any other investment.

Read the full article and ask yourself: do we have a real AI strategy, or just AI activity?

The core idea challenges how executives think about where AI lives in their daily workflow and decision-making, not as an add-on, but as a dedicated layer of operational visibility.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy a scaling company are the ones who stopped doubting themselves.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a disease to cure. It is not. Research covered in Campaign US makes a compelling case that the internal discomfort high performers feel is actually a signal worth listening to, not suppressing.

Here is what that means for leaders running $50M+ organizations:

1. Self-doubt at scale keeps you curious. Leaders who feel like they have nothing left to prove stop asking hard questions. The ones who stay slightly unsettled keep pressure-testing assumptions.

2. The feeling of not belonging in the room often means you are in the right room. Growth requires operating ahead of your current capabilities. Discomfort is a feature, not a flaw.

3. The goal is not confidence without doubt. It is action despite doubt. That distinction separates leaders who scale from leaders who stall.

The companies that plateau between $50M and $500M rarely do so because of market conditions. They do so because the person at the top got comfortable.

When did you last feel genuinely out of your depth, and what did you do with it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fast Company argues that embracing imposter syndrome, rather than fighting it, can actually make you a sharper, more effective leader.

We agree. And we would take it further.

For companies scaling past $50M, the leadership psychology of the person at the top is not a soft issue. It is a structural one. When a CEO or senior executive mismanages their internal doubt, it shows up in decision delay, over-delegation, or the opposite problem: bulldozing teams to mask insecurity.

Scaling is not just an operational challenge. It is a psychological one.

If you lead a growth-stage company and want to understand how your mindset is either accelerating or limiting your trajectory, this article is worth your time.

post3.text:
What does imposter syndrome have to do with scaling a $100M business?

More than most leaders want to admit.

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business, titled 'How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?', was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo. It takes on one of the most common and least discussed forces working against leaders in high-growth companies: the psychological weight of operating at a level that still feels borrowed.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter is this: the question is not whether you experience imposter syndrome at scale. You will. The question is whether your organization is structured to survive what you do with it.

That reframe alone is worth the chapter.

Rock Your Business, the new book from Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, is available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy their companies are the ones who never plan their own life.

Every founder scaling past $50M has a growth plan, a financial model, and a succession roadmap. Almost none of them have a personal life plan. That gap is where burnout, bad decisions, and unexpected exits come from.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this point sharply: founders spend enormous energy planning for growth but almost never plan for what comes after. The same blind spot applies mid-journey.

Three things high-growth leaders consistently ignore:

1. At what point does more revenue cost you more than it gives you?
2. What does your business need to run without your constant presence?
3. What do you actually want the next decade of your life to look like?

Work-life design is not a wellness topic. It is a business performance topic. Leaders who define what they want personally make sharper strategic decisions professionally.

What would change in your business if you treated your own life plan with the same rigor you apply to your P&L?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur made a point that every scaling founder should sit with: almost no one plans for the exit, even when they spend years planning for growth.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. The operational machine gets refined. The team gets built. The revenue climbs. But the leader has never asked what the end state is supposed to look like, for the business or for themselves.

That absence of personal clarity creates real strategic risk. Decisions about hiring, capital, and partnerships get made without a true north.

If you are scaling right now and have not defined what the finish line means to you personally, this article is worth your time.

post3.text:
A recent Entrepreneur article noted that founders pour everything into planning for growth and almost nothing into planning for what comes next. That tension sits at the center of Chapter 10 in our upcoming book.

Chapter 10, Coming Up for Air, was written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain. It addresses something most business books skip entirely: the leader behind the business, not just the business itself.

One idea from that chapter that tends to stop people cold is this: the version of you that got the company to $50M may not be the version of you that can take it to $500M, and the gap between those two versions is not a strategy problem. It is a life design problem.

There is a framework inside that chapter for working through exactly that. We will leave the details for the book.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most $50M+ leaders have a five-year plan for their company and no plan at all for their own life. That is not a personal failure. It is a structural blind spot built into how founders are taught to think. And at scale, that blind spot stops being a personal problem and starts showing up in your hiring, your strategy, and your staying power.
